**Equipment cost:** $60 000 **Salvage value (end of life):** $10 000 **Useful life:** 5 years **Accounting standard:** U.S. GAAP --- ## 1. Straight‑Line Depreciation | Year | Depreciation Expense | Accumulated Depreciation | Book Value at year‑end | |------|---------------------|--------------------------|------------------------| | 1 | **$10,000** | $10,000 | $50,000 | | 2 | **$10,000** | $20,000 | $40,000 | | 3 | **$10,000** | $30,000 | $30,000 | | 4 | **$10,000** | $40,000 | $20,000 | | 5 | **$10,000** | $50,000 | $10,000 (salvage) | *Straight‑line* spreads the depreciable amount evenly over the asset’s useful life. The annual expense is constant: \[ \text{Expense} = \frac{\text{Cost – Salvage}}{\text{Useful Life}} = \frac{60\,000-10\,000}{5}= \$10,000 \] --- ## 2. Double‑Declining Balance (DDB) with Switch to Straight‑Line When Advantageous **Step 1 – Compute the DDB rate:** \( \displaystyle \text{Rate} = \frac{2}{\text{Useful Life}} = \frac{2}{5}=40\% \) **Step 2 – Apply DDB each year until the depreciation that would bring the book value below salvage is reached; then switch to straight‑line (or simply adjust to reach salvage).** | Year | Beginning Book Value | DDB Depreciation (40 %) | Straight‑Line Depreciation (if applied) | Actual Expense* | Accumulated Depreciation | Ending Book Value | |------|---------------------|------------------------|------------------------------------------|-----------------|--------------------------|-------------------| | 1 | $60,000 | $24,000 | $10,000 | **$24,000** | $24,000 | $36,000 | | 2 | $36,000 | $14,400 | $6,500 | **$14,400** | $38,400 | $21,600 | | 3 | $21,600 | $8,640 | $3,867 | **$8,640** | $47,040 | $12,960 | | 4 | $12,960 | $5,184 (would drop below salvage) | $1,480 | **$2,960** (adjusted to reach salvage) | $50,000 | $10,000 | | 5 | $10,000 | – | – | **$0** | $50,000 | $10,000 | \*The “Actual Expense” column shows the amount actually recorded. In year 4 the DDB calculation would have taken the book value to $7,776 (below the required salvage of $10,000). GAAP requires that depreciation not reduce the asset below its salvage value, so we adjust the expense in year 4 to bring the book value exactly to $10,000. After that point no further depreciation is needed. --- ## 3. Expense‑Recognition Patterns & Why a Company Might Prefer One Over the Other | Method | Pattern of Expense Recognition | Typical Rationale for Use | |--------|---------------------------------|---------------------------| | **Straight‑Line** | Equal expense each year (constant $10,000). | • Simplicity and ease of calculation.
• Matches assets that provide a uniform benefit over time (e.g., office furniture, software with steady usage).
• Predictable impact on earnings. | | **Double‑Declining Balance** | High expense in early years, tapering off; front‑loaded depreciation. | • Accelerates the recognition of cost when an asset is expected to lose value quickly or become obsolete (e.g., computers, vehicles).
• Reduces taxable income earlier, providing a tax shield.
• Better matches expense with the pattern of economic benefit if the asset’s productivity declines rapidly in the first few years. | **Why choose DDB?** - **Tax strategy:** Higher depreciation early reduces taxable profit sooner, deferring taxes to later periods when cash flows may be stronger. - **Matching principle:** If an asset’s utility or technological relevance diminishes quickly, front‑loading expense better reflects its economic reality. **Why choose Straight‑Line?** - **Consistency & comparability:** Investors and analysts often prefer the predictability of straight‑line depreciation for budgeting and forecasting. - **Regulatory simplicity:** GAAP allows either method; straight‑line is straightforward to audit and explain. In practice, a company will select the method that best aligns with the asset’s expected pattern of use and its financial or tax planning objectives.
